analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 25% tax on stock buybacks by large oil and gas companies while gasoline prices stay high.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2026 with 16 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has received no hearing, no markup, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the existing federal tax on corporate stock buybacks from 1% to 25% for large oil and gas companies — those with over $1 billion in average annual revenue that make most of their money from producing, refining, processing, transporting, or distributing oil and gas. The higher tax would kick in when the bill takes effect and stay in place until regular gasoline falls below $2.937 per gallon for five straight weeks, as measured by the federal Energy Information Administration. The idea is to tax the extra profits oil companies pocket when pump prices are high, rather than letting them spend that money buying back their own stock.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and drivers. When gasoline prices spike, oil companies often earn outsized profits and use them to buy back their own shares, which shrinks the supply of stock and boosts share prices and executive payouts without lowering anything at the pump. This bill would take a quarter of the value of those buybacks as federal revenue during high-price periods, and the design is meant to push companies toward investing in more fuel supply instead. The revenue would go to the Treasury, easing the tax burden on everyone else.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the stock-buyback excise tax from 1% to 25% for covered oil and gas corporations — companies averaging at least $1 billion in annual gross receipts over three years that are primarily engaged in oil or natural gas production, refining, processing, transportation, or distribution.

The 25% rate applies to buybacks after enactment and stays in effect until the weekly retail price of regular gasoline is below $2.937 per gallon for every week of any 5-consecutive-week period, as determined by the Energy Information Administration — so the tax lifts itself when pump prices normalize.
The special rule apportions the existing buyback-tax credit across the year, so companies cannot avoid the higher rate by timing repurchases within a single taxable year.
Sixteen Democratic senators joined Senator Wyden as cosponsors on the day of introduction, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer.

analysis.who_pays: Large oil and gas corporations — including major producers, refiners, and pipeline and distribution companies — and their shareholders, who would pay 25 cents of tax per dollar of stock repurchased during high-price periods. A buyback tax is legally charged to the corporation but its economic cost lands mainly on the shareholders who sell into the buyback and on executives whose pay is tied to share prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big oil companies and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: The bill does not directly lower gasoline prices; it taxes buybacks after the fact, and whether it changes company behavior or just produces modest revenue depends on how companies respond.

The trigger is set by the retail price of gasoline, which is driven by many factors beyond oil company actions, so the 25% rate could apply (or lapse) in ways that track pump prices rather than any company's actual profits.
The bill covers only oil and gas companies; other large corporations would continue repurchasing stock at the standard 1% rate, so the tax treats one industry differently from the rest.
Pension funds and retirement savers hold large blocks of oil company stock and would bear some of the cost of the higher buyback tax.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but modest: a 25% tax on a narrow slice of corporate behavior — buybacks by one industry during high-price periods — with no estimate of revenue in the record. The main honest objection is targeting: tying the tax to retail gasoline prices is a rough proxy for windfall profits, and exempting other industries from the same treatment is hard to defend on pure tax-policy grounds. On the other side, the cost falls almost entirely on oil company shareholders during exactly the periods when the industry is earning windfall profits, so the tradeoff weighs in favor of the bill for ordinary people. Its practical impact, however, is limited by its narrow scope and by the fact that it has not advanced at all.

outcome.mechanism: The bill has been sitting with the Senate Finance Committee since it was introduced in May 2026, with no hearing or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Senator Ron Wyden introduced the bill on May 20, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.
Sixteen Democratic senators signed on as original cosponsors, including Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Finance Committee members, but no Republican sponsor appears in the record.
The bill's complete action history shows only two actions — introduction and referral to Finance — with no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action since.
The Senate's agenda is controlled by the Republican majority, and the Finance Committee is chaired by a Republican senator, so committee action on the bill has been up to that chair.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large oil and gas companies are better off as things stand: the buyback tax remains at 1% for everyone, and they can continue repurchasing stock during high-price periods without the 25% levy. Drivers and taxpayers gain nothing from the bill's stall, since the tax never takes effect.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.role: Lead sponsor; senior member of the Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and drafted the 25% buyback tax for large oil and gas companies tied to a gasoline-price trigger.

for.name: 16 Democratic senators including Chuck Schumer, Sheldon Whitehouse, and Richard Blumenthal
for.role: Original cosponsors, signed on the day of introduction
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, adding their names in support the same day it was introduced.

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it; no committee action appears in the record.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Affected industry; major lobbying presence in Washington
against.what_they_did: The industry has historically opposed windfall-profit and buyback tax proposals of this kind; no direct action on this bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-controlled Senate Finance Committee has taken no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Large integrated oil and gas producers
industries.note: These companies would pay 25% — up from 1% — on every dollar of stock they repurchase during periods when gasoline tops $2.937 a gallon, directly reducing the value of buybacks that boost share prices and executive compensation. Their interest in keeping the 1% rate runs against drivers and taxpayers, since the buybacks they favor return windfall profits to shareholders rather than to consumers or the Treasury.

industries.industry: Refiners and midstream companies (pipelines, processing, transport, distribution)
industries.note: The bill's definition sweeps in companies engaged in refining, processing, transportation, or distribution of oil and gas, not just extraction, so pipeline operators and refiners with over $1 billion in revenue would also face the 25% rate — even when pump-price spikes stem from forces they do not control.

industries.industry: Publicly traded companies outside oil and gas
industries.note: Their buybacks stay taxed at the existing 1% rate while their oil-and-gas competitors face 25%, a relative advantage — though it comes from being carved out of the bill rather than from anything the bill does for them.

analysis.trajectory: With only Democratic cosponsors, a Republican Senate majority, and no committee action in the months since referral, the bill is very likely to die in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote, as happens to most bills introduced late in a Congress by the minority party. A realistic best case is attachment of similar buyback or windfall-tax language to a broader tax bill, which the record gives no sign of.
